title: Caro-Kann Advance: winning the c5 race

objective.summary: You played 3.e5 for space. Meet Black's ...c5 break with your pieces already placed, not with your king still in the centre.

planClasses.label: Support the chain (c3)
planClasses.description: Play c3 and Be2/Be3 so ...c5 never wins the d4 pawn; slower, but the space advantage keeps.

planClasses.label: Trade the base (dxc5)
planClasses.description: Meet ...c5 by taking, aiming to hold the extra pawn or return it for development; sharper, punishes slow Black play.

planClasses.label: Harass the bishop (h4-h5)
planClasses.description: Chase the light-squared bishop before finishing development; space and a target, at the cost of tempo and king safety.

annotations: The whole point of the Caro-Kann: the bishop leaves before ...e6 shuts it in. Nothing else Black plays here is as testing.
Develop first. The Short System: modest, sound, and it keeps every plan available.
Unassuming. The bishop is not worse than on d3, and it clears the way to castle before the break arrives.
The thematic break. Black hits the base of the chain; every White plan in this pack is an answer to this move.
Hold the centre and finish developing. The pack's model answer: the tension favours the side who is ready for it.
The Tal move: chase the bishop immediately. Enticing and genuinely dangerous, but it spends the tempo you may need when ...c5 lands.
The critical reply. Now g4 is a real idea and so is a later Nf3-g5; but White has committed a wing pawn before castling.
Black strikes at once, before developing the bishop. Practically common below 2000 and a different problem: the grab is available.
Taking is critical. Holding the pawn needs concrete play; giving it back for development is often the mature choice.

checkpoints.label: Choose your plan before the break lands
You are past the authored line

deviations.note: 4.Bd3 invites the trade of Black's good bishop. Playable and popular, but it gives up the pair and a tempo after ...Bxd3.
4.Nc3 keeps g4 ideas alive. A different pack's subject; here it leaves the c5 race unaddressed.
c3 is the other main answer and reaches the same teaching point: the break is met by preparation, not panic.
Taking here is not refuted, but with Be2 already played the recapture race favours Black's development. Play it out and compare.
Castling into the break is not a blunder, but it ignores the objective: the centre resolves while your pieces are not ready.

feedbackClaims.text: ...c5 attacks the base of the pawn chain. Whoever is better developed when it lands usually wins the resulting tension.
4.h4 gains space on the wing but spends the tempo you need to meet ...c5 with a developed piece.
